title: Social Media Compliance for Loan Officers: What to Post
description: A practical social media compliance guide for loan officers: Reg Z triggering terms, Regulation N, comments and DMs, agent co-marketing, and safe post ideas.
keywords: social media compliance for loan officers
image_alt: A person typing on a laptop at a desk beside a window

faq.q: Do mortgage advertising rules apply to a loan officer's personal social media?
faq.a: If a post promotes mortgage credit, it's generally treated as a commercial communication, no matter the platform. Regulation Z advertising rules and Regulation N's ban on misrepresentations can both apply, along with your state and company policies.

faq.q: What are triggering terms in a mortgage ad?
faq.a: Under Regulation Z, triggering terms in a closed-end credit ad include the down payment amount or percentage, the number of payments or repayment period, a payment amount, and the dollar amount of a finance charge. Using one requires additional clear and conspicuous disclosures.

faq.q: Can I answer a rate question in my comments?
faq.a: It's safer not to. A specific rate posted publicly is still advertising and is rarely accurate for that person. Reply warmly and move the conversation to a private channel where you can give a properly disclosed quote.

body_html:
Here's a question I hear from new loan officers every year: "Can I just post that rates dropped this week and tell people to call me?" It sounds harmless. It's the kind of post that fills feeds every Monday. And depending on how it's worded, it can turn a quick caption into a regulated mortgage advertisement with disclosure requirements the author never thought about.

Social media is one of the best tools a loan officer has for staying visible with past clients, agents, and their own network. It's also where I see well-meaning originators get into trouble fastest, because a post feels casual even when the rules treat it like an ad. This is the framework I teach my team so they can post often, post confidently, and stay on the right side of the rules.

Your post is an advertisement, even if it doesn't feel like one

The federal rules don't carve out an exception for Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn, TikTok, or a text blast. If you're promoting mortgage credit, it's a commercial communication. Two sets of rules matter most:

  • Regulation Z advertising rules (Truth in Lending). The CFPB's official commentary to Regulation Z §1026.24 explains when certain words in an ad trigger additional disclosures, and how those disclosures must be made clear and conspicuous, including in internet ads.
  • Regulation N, the Mortgage Acts and Practices Advertising rule. 12 CFR Part 1014 prohibits misrepresentations about the terms of mortgage credit products in any commercial communication. The CFPB's recent Federal Register notice on the rule also restates that covered persons must keep related records for 24 months from last dissemination.

On top of that, your state license and your company's compliance policy will usually spell out what identifying information has to appear in your marketing. If you're not sure what yours requires, ask before you post, not after.

Know the triggering terms before you write the caption

Here's the part most new originators have never heard of. Under Regulation Z, certain details in a closed-end credit ad are "triggering terms." Once you use one, the ad has to include a fuller set of disclosures, stated clearly. According to the CFPB commentary, the categories are:

  • The amount or percentage of a down payment
  • The number of payments or the period of repayment, such as stating a loan's term in years
  • The amount of any payment
  • The dollar amount of any finance charge

Two details catch people off guard. First, a term doesn't have to be stated outright to count. The commentary notes that a phrase implying a down payment, such as advertising a financing percentage, can trigger the rule because the down payment is "readily determinable." Second, some general phrases don't trigger it. The commentary gives "no downpayment" and the annual percentage rate on its own as examples that don't, by themselves, require the extra disclosures. That doesn't make them a free pass; they still have to be accurate and not misleading.

My practical rule for the team: if a caption includes a number tied to a loan, it goes to compliance before it goes live. Most great posts don't need one anyway.

Five habits that keep your feed out of trouble

These come from years of reviewing marketing with loan officers at every experience level. None of them are complicated. They just have to become automatic.

  1. Teach, don't quote. "Here's how a rate lock works" is education. "Lock this rate today" is an ad with terms. Educational content builds more trust anyway.
  2. Point to public sources for market news. If you want to talk about where rates are trending, cite and link a public benchmark like Freddie Mac's weekly Primary Mortgage Market Survey and make clear it's a national average, not something you're offering.
  3. Skip savings comparisons. The commentary treats statements like a claimed monthly savings as implied comparisons, which carry their own requirements for dwelling-secured loans. "Refi and save every month" is the kind of line to rewrite.
  4. Drop the absolutes. Superlatives about pricing and promises of certainty don't belong in mortgage marketing. Nobody can promise approval, a rate, or a closing date, and a post that implies it invites a misrepresentation problem under Regulation N.
  5. Keep a copy of everything. Screenshots, captions, dates, and any paid boosts. Your company may archive automatically, but your own record helps when someone asks what you posted and when.

Comments, DMs, and agent co-marketing

The post itself is only half of it. The conversations underneath are where most of the real risk shows up.

When someone comments "what's your rate right now?", resist answering in public. A specific number in a comment thread is still advertising, and it's almost never accurate for that person anyway. Reply warmly and move it to a private conversation where you can ask the right questions and give a properly disclosed quote.

Co-marketing with real estate agents deserves its own care. A shared open-house flyer or a joint homebuyer video can be great, but the costs and the content need to be handled in a way that respects RESPA. I covered how to set those partnerships up the right way in How Loan Officers Build a Realtor Referral Network That Lasts, and the same principles apply online: split costs fairly, keep it educational, and get compliance approval before anything goes out.

Finally, don't let a reshared post get past you. If an agent tags you in their listing post with financing details you didn't approve, ask them to remove the tag or edit the copy.

What great compliant content actually looks like

The good news is that the content that performs best for loan officers is usually the safest. People want to understand the process, and they remember the person who explained it well. A few ideas my team uses regularly:

  • Short videos answering one buyer question, like the difference between pre-qualified and pre-approved
  • "Myth vs. fact" carousels on credit, down payment programs, or closing costs, with general program facts only
  • A weekly market recap that cites a named public source and links it
  • Behind-the-scenes posts about what happens between application and closing
  • Spotlights on local agents, small businesses, and community events, with their permission

If you want ideas on how to frame rates for nervous buyers without quoting anything, How to Talk to Buyers About Interest Rates Without Scaring Them translates well to social captions too.

The takeaway

Social media rewards consistency, and so does compliance. Treat every post as an ad, know the triggering terms cold, lead with education, cite public sources for market talk, and send anything with a loan-specific number through review first. Do that and you can show up every day without worrying about what's sitting in your feed.

This post is general information, not legal advice. Your company's compliance team and your state regulator have the final word on what your marketing requires. And if you're a loan officer looking for a team that builds this kind of training, support, and review into how it works every day, I'd be glad to talk.
